# Fewer Faults Are Not Enough: Feedback, Timeliness and Device Parallelism in Predictive OS Paging

*Draft for an undergraduate research / regional IEEE conference. G.K Shreyas Bharadwaj (24BCE2256), Vaastav Bajanthri (24BCE2223), P. Giphy Bershan (24BCE2201).*
*Every number below is from `docs/RESULTS.md` (section given in brackets) and is regenerated by the scripts listed there. Status: draft 1, 19 Oct 2026; to be reviewed by the team.*

---

## Abstract

Prefetching pages before they are requested can remove page faults that no eviction policy can avoid, but on a full memory every prefetch evicts a page, so a wrong guess can create a fault.
We study a trace-driven paging simulator that combines a bounded Markov-chain predictor, Linux-style sequential readahead and a cost-aware decision engine driven by measured fault delta.
On 22 real benchmark traces (SPEC CPU 2006 and GAP graph workloads, 44 memory configurations) the final system removes on average 55.0% of LRU's page faults, against 50.7% for readahead alone and 7.7% for Markov prefetching alone, and is worse than LRU in 1 of 44 configurations (by 3.3%).
Four findings matter more than the headline. (1) Prefetch precision is a misleading feedback signal under eviction pressure, and a cheap ghost-list estimate of the fault delta is biased in the same way; an ID-only shadow directory measures it exactly and can be hash-sampled to 1/8 without changing decisions.
(2) Timeliness dominates accuracy: Markov prefetching cuts faults by 35-37% on two SPEC workloads yet is not faster under an I/O-timeline model, because its prefetches arrive late.
(3) In estimated time the final system ties readahead (1.43x vs 1.44x over LRU on an 8-channel NVMe model): the extra faults it removes are paid for with extra reads.
(4) On a single-channel disk model every prefetcher is slower than LRU. We frame this as an evaluation study; the components (Markov prefetching, readahead, fault-rate feedback, ghost and shadow lists) are known.

## 1. Introduction

Classical paging is reactive: it waits for a fault and decides only which page to evict (FIFO, LRU, Clock; Belady's OPT is the offline optimum). Prefetching is proactive, and it is a bet.
A right guess removes a fault, including compulsory first-touch faults that even OPT pays. A wrong guess wastes a read and, when memory is full, evicts a page that may be needed sooner.
A prefetcher therefore needs a predictor and a decision layer that knows when to stop.

We ask three questions with one simulator and identical inputs for every policy:
which feedback signal should drive the decision layer; does a lower fault count translate into lower run time; and how does a learned predictor compare with the simple sequential readahead that operating systems already ship.

**Contributions** (an evaluation study plus two mechanisms, not new algorithms):
1. An evaluation of feedback signals for cost-aware prefetching at page granularity: confidence cannot gate (its floor is structural), precision misleads, a ghost-list fault-delta estimate is biased upward, and an ID-only shadow directory gives the exact per-epoch fault delta at about 0.2% of memory, samplable with SHARDS-style hashing.
2. A combination of sequential readahead with a delta-based Markov predictor that covers both new pages in a run and repeating gap patterns, with the lowest fault count of all systems tested on 22 traces.
3. An I/O-timeline time model and a break-even prefetch cost showing where fault reductions do and do not become speedups (prefetch distance, device parallelism, prediction cost).
4. A set of negative results with diagnoses (prefetch-aware eviction, predictor protection, confidence smoothing, longer stream thresholds).

## 2. Background and related work

- **Markov prefetching**: Joseph and Grunwald, *Prefetching using Markov predictors*, ISCA 1997. Our predictor is a bounded variant (256 contexts, top-2 successors, periodic decay) plus a delta (gap) table.
- **Feedback on fault rate**: Page Fault Frequency (PFF) adapts allocation to the measured fault rate; our controller adapts a prefetch threshold to the measured fault *delta* instead.
- **Prefetch-aware insertion**: PACMan (Wu et al., MICRO 2011) and Linux's inactive list insert prefetched lines/pages at low priority. Our attempt at prefetch-aware eviction did not help (section 6.4).
- **Ghost and shadow lists**: ARC (Megiddo and Modha, FAST 2003) and Linux `mm/workingset.c` keep IDs of evicted pages; SHARDS (Waldspurger et al., FAST 2015) samples pages by hash to approximate cache behaviour cheaply. We use both ideas for the feedback signal.
- **Baselines**: ARC; LRU-2 (O'Neil et al., SIGMOD 1993); Linux-style readahead (window doubles on a sequential stream).
- **Ten recent works** we position against (database buffer prefetching, learned page replacement, spatial prefetching across page boundaries, transformer and graph prefetchers, runtime prefetcher selection, indirect-access prefetching, application-aware virtual memory, profile-guided prefetch): they are domain-specific, eviction-only, spatial-only or need application changes; see `docs/REVIEW_PREP.md` section 2 for the comparison table. *(Full citations to be added by the team.)*

## 3. System design

Per memory access: (1) the memory engine checks residency and handles a fault through the eviction policy; (2) the predictor learns the transition just seen and proposes candidates with a confidence; (3) the decision engine approves or rejects each candidate; (4) approved prefetches enter memory through the same install path as demand faults, so a broken predictor can slow the system but never make it incorrect.

**Predictors.** *Hybrid Markov*: order-2 page Markov, then order-1, then a stride detector (first answer wins; all tables learn on every access). *Delta Markov*: the same bounded table over page gaps, so one entry covers a pattern anywhere in the address space and can predict pages never seen. *Readahead*: two consecutive pages start a stream; the window (initially 4 pages) doubles when the program reaches its middle, capped at a quarter of memory. *Final predictor*: readahead window first, then the delta-hybrid Markov guess.

**Decision engine.** A threshold on confidence when memory is full (any confidence above 0.15 is accepted while frames are free). Every epoch the threshold is lowered if prefetching is winning (fault-delta rate above a dead band) and raised if losing. Readahead candidates carry confidence `run/(run+1)`, so the controller can stop short streams.

**Feedback signals compared.** (a) precision (fraction of prefetches used); (b) oracle: a full shadow copy of memory without prefetching; (c) ghost list: remember pages a prefetch evicted, count refaults within 2,000 accesses, estimate = used prefetches - harmful refaults; (d) **shadow directory**: a no-prefetch copy of the eviction policy holding page IDs only, optionally over a hash-sampled fraction `s` of pages with `s x frames` entries, estimate = (directory faults - real faults on sampled pages) / s.

**Frozen configuration.** Predictor: capacity 256, 2 successors, order 2, decay every 25,000 updates (chosen in Stage 3). Controller (final): epoch 1,000 accesses, step 0.1, dead band 0.002, no prefetch budget cap, chosen on the warm-up portion only (section 4).

## 4. Methodology

**Traces.** ML-DPC LoadTraces: last-level-cache load addresses from SPEC CPU 2006 (bwaves s0-s2, leslie3d s0-s2, milc, libquantum, mcf, soplex, omnetpp, astar, GemsFDTD, lbm, sphinx3) and GAP (bfs-3, bfs-10, pr-3, pr-10, bc-3, cc-5, sssp-3), 200,000 accesses each, mapped to 4 KB pages. Plus six synthetic traces with known structure (sequential, strided, cyclic, clustered, random, phase-changing) used as correctness tests. *These are cache-level traces treated at page granularity: an approximation of OS paging, not OS paging traces.*

**Memory.** Sized as a fraction (1% and 5%) of each trace's working set (8 to 1,163 frames). With fixed large frame counts every policy is identical because nothing is evicted.

**Protocol.** Every design choice and parameter was chosen on the first 25% (time-ordered) of each trace and then evaluated once on the full trace, with a selection rule fixed before each sweep (keep settings whose worst case is within 0.002 of the current one, take the highest mean, keep the current setting unless beaten by more than 0.002).
The traces are deterministic, so repeated runs are identical; robustness comes from 22 traces, 3 segments of two programs and 2 memory sizes. A local rerun on freshly downloaded traces reproduced all 48 rows of the original Colab ablation exactly. 24 automated tests check invariants (OPT is never beaten; LRU and OPT never worsen with more memory; with prefetching off every simulator equals plain LRU) and pin reference numbers.

**Metrics.** `vs_LRU = (LRU faults - faults) / LRU faults`; break-even prefetch cost `c* = (LRU faults - faults) / prefetches`; and estimated speedup `time(LRU) / time(system)` from an I/O timeline (section 6.5).

## 5. Results: the decision layer (Markov predictor, 8 configurations)

**Confidence cannot gate prefetching** [RESULTS 1, 3]. No prediction has confidence below 0.5, so a 0.3 threshold is bitwise identical to always prefetching. This is structural: the top one of at most two successors always holds at least half of the counts.

**Precision misleads under eviction pressure** [RESULTS 3]. Over all runs precision correlates with benefit (+0.73), but on the clustered trace with 9 frames four deciders reached precision 0.81-0.86 and still increased faults; eviction inflation tracked harm, precision did not. A used prefetch can displace a page needed sooner.

**Fault-delta feedback** [RESULTS 3]. Against always prefetching it halves the worst case (-0.72% vs -1.50%) and keeps 99.94% of the benefit on leslie3d (35.0% fewer faults than LRU). The gain is the same on FIFO, LRU and Clock (34.5-38.6%) [RESULTS 4].

**The ghost list reproduces the oracle for the Markov predictor** (mean gain 0.0902 vs 0.0898) [RESULTS 5], but is biased upward when readahead is added: on clustered@9 it reports winning in 24 of 25 epochs (estimated delta +988) while the true delta is -1,250, and the system ends 21.5% worse than LRU [RESULTS 12].
The **shadow directory** measures the true delta exactly and cuts that loss to 2.5%; with 1/8 hash sampling, fault counts were unchanged on 9 of 10 real traces at 5% memory [RESULTS 13].

## 6. Results: predictors, baselines, robustness and time

### 6.1 Stronger baselines [RESULTS 9]
ARC and LRU-2 alone do not close the LRU-OPT gap (ARC is 8% worse than LRU on leslie3d at 21 frames; LRU-2 is much worse on leslie3d and bwaves, confirmed against an independent implementation).
Prediction still adds 34-36% on top of ARC on leslie3d and bwaves. **Linux-style readahead beats Markov prefetching on 3 of the original 4 real traces** (bwaves 204 vs 1,969 faults; bfs-3 2,924 vs 7,427; pr-3 2,905 vs 5,872), because it fetches new pages in a run, which a page-number Markov model cannot predict.

### 6.2 Combining readahead and delta-Markov [RESULTS 9-10]
On leslie3d at 21 frames the combination cuts faults from 15,313 (LRU) and 11,624 (readahead) to 8,131; adding the delta tier helps Markov alone on bwaves (1,969 to 810 faults).

### 6.3 Robustness: 22 real traces, 44 points [RESULTS 16]

| System | Mean vs LRU | Median | Worst | Worse than LRU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Original Markov + ghost decider | +7.7% | +1.5% | -0.3% | 1/44 |
| Linux-style readahead | +50.7% | +55.0% | -19.3% | 2/44 |
| **Final system** | **+55.0%** | **+59.3%** | **-3.3%** | **1/44** |

The final system has fewer faults than readahead in 34 of 44 points, ties in 8 and loses in 2 (one by a single fault; sphinx3 at 1% by 16.9% of LRU's faults, where the decider holds back useful streams). It is below OPT in 30 of 44 points, which is possible because prefetching removes compulsory faults.
lbm has no predictable pattern (no system gains); milc and libquantum are pure streaming, where all gain comes from readahead.

### 6.4 What did not work [RESULTS 9, 13]
Evicting unused prefetches early never beat LRU (and protecting prefetches longer was much worse); protecting the predicted next page changed nothing (it is almost always resident and recent already); a longer minimum stream length fixed the synthetic clustered case only by losing the graph gains; smoothing confidence was slightly worse; an "off" state with exponential-backoff probing never triggered. A 35% prefetch budget cap inherited from the first design was found to block the system on omnetpp while it was winning every epoch and was removed (choice made on warm-up data).

### 6.5 Time [RESULTS 14, 16]
An I/O timeline replays every run: compute time per traced access (unknown for these traces, swept 0.1-10 us), 0.2 us of prediction cost per access, 4 KB reads of 80 us on an NVMe model with 8 parallel channels or 5 ms on a single-channel HDD model. Demand faults block and can queue behind prefetch reads; a prefetched page used before its read completes stalls for the rest.

| Geometric-mean speedup vs LRU (1 us compute) | NVMe, 8 channels | HDD, 1 channel |
|---|---|---|
| Original Markov | 0.97x (slower on 18/22) | 0.93x |
| Readahead | 1.44x (slower on 2/22) | 0.80x |
| Final system | 1.43x (slower on 3/22) | 0.70x |

Three readings. *Timeliness*: Markov prefetching cuts faults 35-37% on leslie3d and bwaves yet is not faster, because it prefetches one access ahead and 16-22% of run time becomes waiting on late prefetches; readahead fetches a window ahead. *Faults vs time*: the final system's extra fault reduction over readahead is paid for with extra reads, so on average the two tie in time (the final system wins on leslie3d, 1.24x vs 1.14x, and loses on sphinx3, 0.93x vs 1.26x). *Device*: on a single-channel disk every prefetch costs a full access and every prefetcher is slower than LRU, consistent with every break-even cost being below 1.

## 7. Discussion

Prediction accuracy, fault count and run time rank systems differently. The most accurate predictor here (Markov, useful rate 0.81 on the first four real traces) gives the smallest speedup; the system with the fewest faults ties the simplest one in time. A prefetcher should therefore be judged by its effect on time under a stated device model, and its decision layer should be fed the true fault delta, which an ID-only directory provides cheaply.
The feedback lesson generalises: precision and the ghost-list estimate share one blind spot, they count a *used* prefetch as a saved fault even when it displaced a page needed sooner.

## 8. Limitations

LLC traces approximate paging; 200,000 accesses per trace and small simulated memories (8-1,163 frames); one run per configuration (deterministic traces). Time figures come from a model with stated latencies, a swept compute time and no demand-read priority, write-back or I/O merging; they are not measurements.
The predictor observes every access, which a kernel cannot (it sees faults and accessed bits), so the prediction cost charged here is an upper bound and the information available is optimistic. ARC drops the textbook tie-break; LRU-2 has no correlated-reference period; the readahead window is a quarter of memory. The SHARDS sampling result is shown only for memories of 13-1,163 frames.

## 9. Conclusion

A cost-aware prefetcher combining readahead and a delta-Markov predictor, steered by an exact, cheap fault-delta signal, removes the most page faults of every system we tested on 22 real traces, and is rarely harmful. But fewer faults are not enough: in estimated time it only matches Linux-style readahead on a parallel SSD and loses to LRU on a single-channel disk. Future work: evaluate on OS-level page-fault traces, add demand-read priority and prefetch distance control, compare against a learned (LSTM/attention) predictor under the same time model, and test directory sampling at realistic memory sizes.
